5: 1. "Menu" sheet: in the green cells, enter each dish with its plate cost, the price it has TODAY in the dining room (pre-tax), the product type, the ceiling price the market accepts and the units you sell per month.
6: 2. "Inputs" sheet: set the commission, packaging per order, dishes per order and target food cost for EACH channel. They're the terms of your contract, not an official rate.
7: 3. Check the tax matrix: the channel and the product type decide the rate, and the formulas read it with INDEX/MATCH. It ships at 0% in all nine cells, the US default.
8: 4. Read "Effective food cost at the dine-in price": it's what your food cost turns into if you list the same price on the app that you charge in the dining room.
9: 5. Compare the "Pre-tax price needed" with your ceiling price. The "Viable?" column flags the dishes that don't fit that channel at your target.
10: 6. "Price you can charge" is the lower of the two: if the price needed goes over the ceiling, you charge the ceiling and the food cost slips; that's where each channel's real monthly margin is.
11: 7. "Summary" sheet: viable dishes, average food cost, monthly margin by channel and the difference from dine-in.
12: 8. Units sold are the same in all three channels on purpose: the question the workbook answers is what margin THAT volume would bring in each channel, not how much you would sell in each one.
14: Every amount is pre-tax except the "Price incl. tax for the guest" column, the price the guest sees on the menu or the app. Amounts carry no currency symbol: they are in your currency.

Tax by market (the nine cells of the tax matrix on "Inputs", 0% by default; the formulas treat the price as tax-inclusive, so don't type a US sales tax there):
• US: menu prices are pre-tax and sales tax is added on the bill. Leave 0% and type pre-tax prices.
• Canada: price before tax, as in the US. Leave 0%.
• UK: printed prices must include VAT. Type 20% for dine-in and hot takeaway food and 0% where cold takeaway food is zero-rated (not soft drinks, confectionery or crisps).
• Australia: prices include GST. Type 10%.
16: Food cost is measured on NET sales (before tax) and on cost NET of any tax you get back: in the US, sales tax you pay on supplies is a cost; if you're registered for VAT or GST/HST, the tax on your purchases is cash flow, not cost.

127: An average food cost far above target in takeout or delivery doesn't mean the channel is bad: it means you're selling at the dining-room price in a channel that charges commission and packaging.
128: With the example data, only 12 of the 20 dishes are viable in delivery: at a 30% commission, even with a 40% target food cost, the price needed breaks the ceiling on the other eight. That's the normal result of taking the dining-room menu to an app without redesigning it, and the way out isn't to lower the target by eye, but a shorter delivery menu, with low-cost dishes and the packaging already built into the price.
129: In dine-in, a "No" doesn't mean you remove the dish: it means that dish doesn't reach your target food cost at the price the market accepts. High-cost dishes (the ribeye, market fish) are priced by MARGIN, not by factor: menu-pricing-calculator.xlsx handles that.
130: If a dish needs a price the market won't pay, you have four ways out: rework it to lower the cost, raise it as far as the ceiling and accept a worse food cost, take it out of that channel, or replace it with a dish designed for that channel.
131: The "Monthly margin" column already charges the price you can really charge (the lower of the price needed and the ceiling): that's why the delivery margin can fall far below dine-in even when you sell the same.
132: The margin on this sheet is CONTRIBUTION margin (net price minus product cost). It doesn't deduct labor or overhead: prime-cost-dashboard.xlsx measures that.
